lead: This unit teaches how machines find groups and useful directions in data with no labels. It moves from clustering families to k-means, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian mixtures and EM, then to PCA, feature selection and LDA. After it you can compute small examples by hand and judge when each method is the right choice.
about: The unit covers unsupervised learning: finding structure in data without labels. Chapter 4.1 sets out clustering families and distance. Chapters 4.2 to 4.4 give hard k-means, hierarchical trees and soft Gaussian mixtures with EM. Chapters 4.5 to 4.7 turn to dimensionality reduction: PCA, feature selection with correlation, and supervised LDA. Chapter 4.8 evaluates clusters, and 4.9 extends to fuzzy memberships. Examples use small numeric data so each step can be checked by hand. After the unit a student can run and explain k-means, read a dendrogram, fit a small GMM, compute principal components, select features and judge a clustering result.

chapters.idea: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data, and clustering groups similar points by a chosen distance.
chapters.depth: Define unsupervised learning, unlabeled data, similarity and distance (Euclidean, Manhattan). Classify clustering by partitional vs hierarchical, hard vs soft, density-based vs model-based. Some syllabi call clustering cluster analysis and list DBSCAN as density-based. Keep formulas out; show one small distance table.

figure.title: Clustering families
figure.aria: A flow from unlabeled data through a similarity measure to clustering, branching into partitional, hierarchical, density-based and soft families.

chapters.example: A shop has 12 customer records with monthly spend in rupees and visits: (1200,2), (1500,3), (4800,8), (5200,9), (900,1), (1100,2), (5000,7), (4600,6), (3000,4), (3200,5), (800,1), (5300,8). Group into two clusters by eye and state whether the grouping is partitional or hierarchical.
chapters.trap: The main trap is calling clustering supervised or using accuracy without labels; also forgetting that distance scaling changes groups.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 types of learning and math review of vectors.
chapters.leave: Algorithm details to 4.2 to 4.4; evaluation to 4.8; dimensionality reduction to 4.5 to 4.7.

chapters.idea: K-means partitions n points into k groups by alternating nearest-centroid assignment and centroid recomputation to minimise within-cluster sum of squares.
chapters.depth: Give the k-means algorithm as Lloyd's algorithm: choose k, initialise centroids, assign each point to nearest centroid, recompute centroids, repeat until assignment stops changing. Define centroid, cluster, within-cluster sum of squares SSE = Σ over clusters Σ over points ||x − μ||². Cover k-means++ idea, scaling, outliers, local minima, elbow and silhouette only as names; leave silhouette to 4.8. Some syllabi call this Lloyd's algorithm.

figure.aria: Four points are assigned to two updated centroids; each point sits 0.5 away from its centroid.

chapters.example: Apply k-means with k=2 to points A(1,1), B(2,1), C(4,4), D(5,4). Start centroids at A(1,1) and D(5,4). Use Euclidean distance; show one assignment step, update the centroids, and give the final clusters. Expected: clusters {A,B} and {C,D}, centroids (1.5,1) and (4.5,4).
chapters.trap: K-means can stop at a local minimum and its result depends on initial centroids and feature scaling; do not confuse k with the number of iterations.
chapters.leave: Gaussian mixtures to 4.4, hierarchical clustering to 4.3, evaluation to 4.8.

chapters.idea: Hierarchical clustering builds a nested tree of clusters by merging closest groups bottom-up or splitting top-down.
chapters.depth: Build agglomerative clustering bottom-up: start with n singleton clusters, merge the pair with smallest linkage distance, repeat; record merge height. Cover single, complete, average and Ward linkage. Show divisive as top-down splitting. Read a dendrogram: leaves are points, joins are merges, height is distance. Some syllabi call this hierarchical cluster analysis.

figure.aria: A dendrogram for five points p1,p2,p4,p8,p9 merges p1 with p2 at height 1, joins p4 at height 2, and joins the p8-p9 pair at height 4.

chapters.example: Five points on a line: 1, 2, 4, 8, 9. Use single-link agglomerative clustering. List the merge heights and cut the dendrogram to get two clusters. Expected merges at heights 1, 1, 2, 4; cut gives {1,2,4} and {8,9}.
chapters.trap: Linkage choice changes the dendrogram; a cut height is a distance, not a cluster count; single-link can chain long clusters.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1; distance from Unit 1 math review.
chapters.leave: K-means details to 4.2, soft clustering to 4.4, evaluation to 4.8.

chapters.idea: A Gaussian mixture models data as a weighted sum of Gaussian components, and EM estimates the hidden component memberships and parameters.
chapters.depth: Define a Gaussian mixture: p(x)=Σ π_k N(x|μ_k,Σ_k), with weights π_k summing to 1. Introduce latent component labels and responsibilities r_ik. Give EM: E-step computes r_ik, M-step updates π, μ, Σ; likelihood is non-decreasing until convergence. Compare soft GMM with hard k-means. Some syllabi call this EM clustering or mixture of Gaussians.

figure.title: EM cycle
figure.aria: EM starts with parameters θ, repeats an E-step for responsibilities and an M-step for parameters until convergence, then outputs soft clusters.

chapters.example: For points 0, 1, 4, fit a two-component one-dimensional GMM with equal weights and variance σ²=1. Initial means are μ1=0 and μ2=4. Run one E-step and one M-step for the means. Expected responsibilities for component 1: about 0.9997, 0.9820, 0.0003; updated means μ1≈0.496 and μ2≈3.946.
chapters.trap: EM maximises likelihood and can stop at a local optimum; responsibilities are probabilities, not hard labels; a variance can collapse to zero if unconstrained.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1; Unit 1 probability distributions; Bayes idea from Unit 3.
chapters.leave: K-means details to 4.2; evaluation to 4.8; fuzzy memberships to 4.9.

chapters.idea: PCA finds new orthogonal axes that capture maximum variance, giving a smaller set of features for the data.
chapters.depth: Mean-centre X, form covariance C = (1/(n−1)) XᵀX, find eigenvalues λ_i and eigenvectors v_i. Sort by λ, keep first k, project Z = X V_k. Define explained variance ratio λ_i/Σλ. Mention standardisation, SVD route, and that PCA is unsupervised. Some syllabi call this the Karhunen–Loève transform.

figure.title: PCA steps
figure.aria: PCA mean-centres the data, forms the covariance matrix, computes eigenvalues and eigenvectors, sorts components by variance and projects data onto the first k.

chapters.example: A two-feature dataset has covariance matrix C = [[4,3],[3,4]]. Find its eigenvalues and unit eigenvectors, state the first principal component, and give the explained variance ratio for the first component. Expected λ=7 and 1; first PC along (1,1)/√2; ratio 7/8=87.5%.
chapters.trap: PCA uses variance only and ignores class labels; components are directions, so signs can flip; always centre and usually scale before PCA.
chapters.leave: LDA to 4.7; feature selection to 4.6; clustering evaluation to 4.8.

chapters.idea: Feature selection keeps a useful subset of original features, and correlation analysis exposes redundant or weakly related features.
chapters.depth: Define feature selection as choosing a subset of original features. Cover filter methods (variance threshold, correlation with target, chi-square, mutual information), wrapper methods (forward selection, backward elimination, RFE), embedded methods (L1 lasso, tree importance). Define Pearson correlation r = cov(X,Y)/(σ_X σ_Y), range −1 to 1; warn that r measures linear association. Some syllabi call this feature subset selection.

figure.title: Correlation matrix
figure.aria: A correlation table for features X1, X2, X3 and target y; the high entries link X1 and X3 with y and with each other.

chapters.example: A dataset has features X1, X2, X3 and target y. Correlations with y: r(X1,y)=0.82, r(X2,y)=0.05, r(X3,y)=−0.78; also r(X1,X3)=−0.91. Using a filter with |r|≥0.5, list selected features and flag redundancy. Expected selected X1 and X3; X1 and X3 are redundant.
chapters.trap: Correlation measures linear association only; a feature can have low correlation with y and still help in a nonlinear model; correlated features may be redundant but not always useless.
chapters.leave: PCA extraction to 4.5; LDA to 4.7; model evaluation to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: LDA is a supervised projection that separates labelled classes by maximising between-class scatter relative to within-class scatter.
chapters.depth: Define LDA for labelled classes: class means μ_c, within-class scatter S_W = Σ_c Σ_{x in c}(x−μ_c)(x−μ_c)ᵀ, between-class S_B. Maximise wᵀS_B w / wᵀS_W w, giving S_W⁻¹S_B w = λw. At most C−1 components for C classes. Compare with PCA: PCA uses variance, LDA uses class separation. Some syllabi call this Fisher's linear discriminant.

figure.aria: Two class means at (0,0) and (4,4); the LDA axis is the line x2 = x1 through them.

chapters.example: Two classes have means μ1=(0,0) and μ2=(4,4); both have identity within-class scatter S_W=I. Find the LDA direction w and the projected class means on the unit direction. Expected direction (1,1) or unit (1,1)/√2; projected means 0 and 4√2≈5.66.
chapters.trap: LDA needs class labels and assumes shared covariance for its simple form; S_W can be singular with few samples; use at most C−1 components.
chapters.leave: PCA derivation to 4.5; classifier training to Unit 3; evaluation to 4.8.

chapters.idea: Clustering evaluation uses internal cohesion and separation, or external labels when they exist, because clusters have no target by default.
chapters.depth: Advanced: only a few universities teach this. Define internal evaluation without labels (cohesion, separation, silhouette, Davies–Bouldin, Calinski–Harabasz) and external evaluation with true labels (purity, Rand index, adjusted Rand, NMI). Show silhouette formula s=(b−a)/max(a,b), range −1 to 1. Keep to one worked silhouette and one table of measures.

figure.aria: Points A and B lie in one cluster one unit apart; C lies in another cluster, 5.66 from A.

chapters.example: Points A(0,0) and B(0,1) are in cluster 1; C(4,4) is in cluster 2. Compute the silhouette score of A using Euclidean distance. Expected a=1, b=√32≈5.657, s=(5.657−1)/5.657≈0.823.
chapters.trap: Without true labels use internal measures; silhouette is in [−1,1] and needs a distance; external measures need ground truth.
chapters.leave: Clustering algorithms to 4.2 to 4.4; model evaluation metrics to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Fuzzy clustering gives every point a membership degree in every cluster instead of one hard assignment.
chapters.depth: Advanced: only a few universities teach this. Define fuzzy membership u_ik in [0,1] with Σ_k u_ik =1 for each point i. Give fuzzy c-means objective Σ_iΣ_k u_ik^m d_ik² with fuzzifier m>1; update memberships and centres; compare with hard k-means. Some syllabi call this fuzzy c-means.

figure.aria: Point x=1 is distance 1 from centre c1=0 and distance 3 from centre c2=4, giving fuzzy memberships 0.90 and 0.10.

chapters.example: For point x=1, cluster centres c1=0 and c2=4, and fuzzifier m=2, compute the fuzzy memberships u1 and u2 using Euclidean distance. Expected d1=1, d2=3, u1=0.90, u2=0.10.
chapters.trap: Memberships sum to 1 for each point; m must be greater than 1; fuzzy output is not a probability unless extra assumptions are made.
chapters.leave: Hard k-means details to 4.2; GMM probability model to 4.4; evaluation to 4.8.

links: distance to centroid leads to k-means
PCA unsupervised axis, LDA supervised axis
correlation finds redundancy; PCA extracts axes
soft membership continues in fuzzy c-means
variance and correlation guide feature choice
